description: We are a multidisciplinary student team combining software development, AI/ML, data science, ECE engineering, and creative design. We use NASA and partner-agency open data to explore space and Earth challenges, uncover meaningful insights, and build practical software solutions. Our strength is combining scientific analysis, engineering, and UI/UX to turn complex space data into clear, interactive,  experiences.
summary:
What happens to a flame when hot air no longer rises? Team Pushpa Boys built FLARE-X, an interactive dashboard that helps users explore this question through NASA’s microgravity combustion research. In the 3D Flame Lab, users can switch a candle from Earth gravity to free fall and see its flame become rounder and bluer. They can then explore measured results, including how quickly flames spread across acrylic in BASS-II and how smoke particles changed size over time in SAME.

The AI guide helps users find relevant investigations, compare what each experiment tested, and trace answers to NASA sources. By connecting each fire-safety question to experimental evidence, FLARE-X helps students and researchers understand how material selection, smoke detection, and flame suppression matter for crew habitats.
details:
FLARE-X — Flame in Freefall

What would a candle look like aboard a spacecraft?

Picture a candle burning on Earth. Its yellow tip stretches upward as hot gases rise. Now switch the Flame Lab to free fall. In still air, the simulated flame becomes rounder and bluer. That change raises a question for anyone designing a crew habitat. If even a candle burns differently in space, how do we decide which materials to use, what a smoke detector should detect, or how to put a fire out?

We are Team Pushpa Boys from SRM, India. We built FLARE-X for the Flame in Freefall challenge to help people explore those questions using NASA’s microgravity combustion research. A student can start with the candle. A researcher can start with a measurement. Both can follow the evidence back to the original report.

How the dashboard works

“The same candle under two simulated conditions. In still air, the tall Earth flame becomes rounder and bluer in free fall.”

Explore a flame. In the interactive 3D Flame Lab, users change gravity and airflow and observe how the candle responds. Planet settings let them explore a simple thought experiment: how might the same flame behave under different gravity if the chamber still supplied air? These scenes are labelled as educational simulations.

Find the right experiment. Users can ask the AI guide, “What is the difference between BASS-II and FLEX?” The answer depends on what is burning and what the researchers measured. BASS-II examined how flames spread across solid materials such as acrylic. FLEX examined how liquid-fuel droplets burned and under what conditions their flames went out. FLARE-X ranks investigations by their relevance to the question and links users to the underlying sources.

Read a real result. In Compare measurements, users can follow smoke from Kapton, a spacecraft insulation material. In NASA’s SAME results, the geometric mean particle diameter increased from 0.042 micrometres in fresh smoke to 0.089 micrometres after 12 minutes. The comparison gives users a concrete reason to ask how a detector responds as smoke ages. They can open Table 2 and check both values themselves. NASA smoke measurement report

How we built it

We built the dashboard with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We organized selected NASA Physical Sciences Informatics records and technical reports by fuel, test conditions, measurements, and fire-safety question. The guide uses those records for study comparisons and numerical lookups. On compatible devices, WebLLM runs a local language model for explanations. Short narrated videos introduce the investigations, and the BASS-II explorer lets users export acrylic test measurements as a CSV for further analysis.

Why it matters

A student who does not know the name Saffire can still ask, “Which experiment studied how a larger fire spreads in a spacecraft?” An engineering team investigating cabin materials can find BASS-II, inspect the airflow and sample dimensions for a particular test, and decide whether those conditions fit its question. FLARE-X makes that path from question to evidence visible while preserving a distinction that matters for crew safety: what the simulator illustrates, what NASA measured, and what still needs testing.

Explore the FLARE-X dashboard
